section_summary: This section documents the rapid reorganization of Japanese political life under the Allied occupation, including the emergence of Liberal, Socialist, Communist, and Progressive parties, debates over constitutional revision and the Emperor system, and concern about conservative continuities. Weekly political summaries describe labor organization, Zaibatsu dissolution, food and housing shortages, unemployment, press reform, and public criticism of wartime leaders. Additional interviews with Seisaburō Shinobu, Tatsuo Morito, and Kyuichi Tokuda examine Japanese expansionism, democratic reform, agrarian and labor policy, and Communist strategy, while Soviet reports offer sharply critical portrayals of postwar Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram 3585: Izvestiya Commentary on the Political Situation in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports an Izvestiya editorial criticizing the Shidehara cabinet and warning that elections without prior institutional reform would preserve Japanese imperialism.
subfiles.summary: Izvestiya welcomes the fall of the Higashikuni government but argues that Shidehara is too closely connected with Japan's imperialist past and monopolistic interests to lead democratic reform. It warns that liberal rhetoric, early elections, and reliance on an unreformed state apparatus could obstruct the Potsdam Declaration and create false confidence in compromised political leaders.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 31: Periodic Report on Political Parties and Movements for the Week Ending October 26, 1945
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser to the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Surveys the formation, programs, personnel, and rivalries of Japan's Liberal, Socialist, Communist, and conservative parties.
subfiles.summary: The report compares emerging Liberal and Socialist programs, Communist attempts to form a popular front, and conservative efforts to reorganize the former Japan Political Association. Its detailed Socialist Party history identifies founding Diet members, internal divisions, and proposals on labor, agriculture, welfare, women, education, and elections. Appendices reproduce a Communist manifesto calling for abolition of the imperial institution and summarize the Liberal and Socialist platforms.

subfiles.title: Request for Declassification or Downgrading of Despatch No. 31
subfiles.from: Wilson C. Flake, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Originating or action division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests review and declassification of the October 27, 1945 political-party despatch.
subfiles.summary: The form identifies Despatch No. 31 from George Atcheson Jr. concerning political-party developments during the week ending October 26, 1945. It records the document's former Secret classification and authorization to change it to Unclassified.

subfiles.title: Telegram 76: General Political Summary
subfiles.about: Provides a broad assessment of Japanese politics, constitutional debate, war responsibility, Zaibatsu policy, economic distress, and occupation reforms.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports that the Liberal, Socialist, and Communist parties are organizing but remain weak outside major centers, while conservative groups are beginning to regroup. Constitutional reform, the responsibility of wartime leaders, newspaper control, and dissolution of the Zaibatsu are increasingly prominent public issues. The Shidehara cabinet is judged passive and constrained by its conservative bureaucratic background, although SCAP directives and American troop conduct are generally well received.

subfiles.title: Telegram 3762: Red Fleet Article on Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes Soviet correspondent I. Baru's hostile portrayal of poverty, hypocrisy, and destruction in occupied Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: A Red Fleet article emphasizes Japanese poverty and ridicules parliamentarians who expressed sympathy for the United States after previously applauding the Pearl Harbor attack. Baru also criticizes wealthy Japanese claims of shared wartime sacrifice and describes Tokyo as a ruined city that deserved the fate it had prepared for others.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on SCAP Contacts with Konoe
subfiles.from: Major General Richard J. Marshall, Acting Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Conveys General MacArthur's instruction that Atcheson cease involvement with Konoe's private constitutional-revision effort.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur believed constitutional revision should proceed through the Japanese government rather than through Konoe's connection to the Imperial Household. Marshall warns that Konoe might publicize his contacts with Atcheson to imply American sponsorship, exposing Atcheson to serious political criticism in the United States.

subfiles.title: Telegram 106: Inquiry on Receipt of Weekly Political Summary
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Department received Atcheson's first weekly political summary, Telegram 76 of October 30.
subfiles.summary: This brief administrative telegram requests confirmation that the Department received the first weekly political summary. It identifies the missing or unacknowledged report as Telegram 76 of October 30.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107: Political Summary, October 31–November 8
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr. for SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington, via WARCOS; repeated to Chungking and Moscow
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese governmental, political, labor, educational, press, economic, and Zaibatsu developments during October 31–November 8.
subfiles.summary: The cabinet created several bodies but continued to talk more than act, while political and labor organization accelerated and SCAP moved to dissolve the major Zaibatsu. The Socialist Party formally organized, Communists expanded their activity, and conservative minor parties proliferated. The report also describes university and press reform, mounting food and housing distress, peaceful demonstrations, and anxiety about reparations.

subfiles.title: Telegram 129: Acknowledgment of Telegram 76
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for George Atcheson Jr.
subfiles.about: Confirms receipt of Atcheson's October 30 weekly political summary.
subfiles.summary: The Department informs Atcheson that his Telegram 76 of October 30 was received in November. The message responds directly to his later inquiry concerning its delivery.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 48: Comments of Japanese Historian Seisaburō Shinobu on Japanese Expansion and Nationalistic Organizations
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with memorandum of conversation and biographical appendix
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Shinobu's analysis of Japanese expansionism, industrial interests, militarism, and nationalist organizations.
subfiles.summary: Shinobu traces Japanese policy after the Russo-Japanese War to competing internationalist and expansionist tendencies, with secret societies influencing expansion in Manchuria and North China. He argues that textile interests initially sought economic control in China, while the growing power of heavy industry brought industrialists into alliance with militarists and strengthened southward expansion after 1937. The memorandum also identifies nationalist organizations and intellectuals involved in popular indoctrination, and an appendix outlines Shinobu's career, imprisonment, and writings.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 50: Views of Japanese Labor Economist Tatsuo Morito on Constitutional Reform and Other Current Problems
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with memorandum of conversation and biographical appendix
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Morito's views on constitutional revision, the Emperor, university reform, political parties, labor, agriculture, and Japan's economic future.
subfiles.summary: Morito argues that constitutional reform must protect popular rights, make the cabinet responsible to the Diet, and reduce the Emperor to a controlled moral symbol without abruptly abolishing the institution. He advocates reinstating politically dismissed professors and warns that weak liberal, socialist, and labor organizations could allow both fascist and Communist extremes to grow. Morito considers renewed industrial production essential both for economic recovery and for building an urban democratic counterweight to conservative peasant society.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 51: Political and Economic Policies of the Japanese Communist Party
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Kyuichi Tokuda's proposals concerning food, unemployment, land, worker control, a Socialist-Communist popular front, and Korean laborers in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tokuda attributes shortages and inflation to capitalist, military, landlord, and elite hoarding, proposing popular inspection committees, direct farmer-worker distribution, and use of Imperial lands and forests. He says the Communists seek immediate reform within capitalism while gradually building a popular front with Socialists and ultimately abolishing the Emperor system. The discussion also covers strikes by Korean and Chinese miners, alleged abuses by mine owners, Communist opposition to violence, and proposals for the orderly repatriation of Koreans.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 60: Political Parties in Japan—Developments During the Week Ending November 17, 1945
subfiles.doc_type: despatch with weekly report and comparative appendix
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the inauguration of the Japan Progressive Party and compares the principles and policies of Japan's four major political parties.
subfiles.summary: The report presents the Progressive Party as a conservative successor to the wartime Political Association of Great Japan, with more than 200 Diet members and likely control of the existing legislature. It describes efforts to exclude particularly compromised wartime politicians, contrasts Progressive controlled capitalism with Liberal laissez-faire and Socialist planning, and notes continued Communist popular-front organizing. The appendix compares Progressive, Liberal, Social Democratic, and Communist positions on the Emperor, constitutional and administrative reform, civil liberties, foreign policy, and economic policy; the comparison continues beyond page 299.
